author: Shareholders Unite
title: The Chinese Strikeback
text:
Markets are reeling under mounting risks of trade war. Some argue that the US is in a good position because it has the least to lose, especially versus China. We're not so sure.
While it is true that China exports much more to the US than the other way around, and this seemingly makes China more vulnerable to a trade war, reality is a bit more complicated than that.
The Chinese have other ways of responding, we will discuss four of these below.
China 2025 Much of the US government's animus is directed at the Chinese project to stimulate its high-tech industries (10 of these are identified), called China 2025. We covered this program in an earlier article so we refer to that for reference.
We argued there that there is nothing special about that program, many countries have ambitions (and policies) to stimulate what they see as sectors of the future.
The US itself has (or, to a large extent had) multiple programs of public funded fundamental research from which many of the new technologies and even whole industries emerged.
The US government now looks set to take Chinese high-tech on directly, from MarketWatch :
President Donald Trump, already embroiled in a trade battle with China, plans to ratchet commercial tensions higher by barring many Chinese companies from investing in U.S. technology firms, and by blocking additional technology exports to Beijing, said people familiar with administration plans.
While at the moment of writing, it isn't actually sure whether this will happen (there were denials from Peter Navarro, Trump's main trade adviser), but would this be a good thing?
This is a bit of a double-edged sword, in our view. It might very well lead to a doubling down of Chinese efforts with respect to China 2025. While there is no doubt that restricted access to American technology is a significant barrier in the short term, longer-term the Chinese could double down on greater independence.
China has the resources to pull this off, like vast numbers of engineers and increasingly sophisticated high-tech and internet companies. The Chinese might also develop less, rather than more respect for US intellectual property in the process.
US companies in China China could also make it more difficult for American companies to operate in China. They have a lot of ways to achieve that, all kinds of administrative burdens could be placed on companies. Here is Politico :
When Beijing was upset over South Korea’s decision last year to deploy a U.S. missile system, it ratcheted up pressure using a tool ripped from the playbook of Western consumer activists: consumer boycotts. A series of government-encouraged boycotts sent sales of South Korean-made Hyundais in China plummeting by more than half, decreased Chinese tourist traffic by more than 60 percent and temporarily shut down 55 supermarkets in China run by the large Korean retailer Lotte...
Major U.S. companies have tied their future fortunes to the Chinese market, with its booming middle class and rising incomes.U.S. investment in China nearly doubled in the six years between 2009 and 2015 and represents a $550 billion market for U.S. goods and services.
“It could get quite ugly,” said Deborah Elms, founder of the Asian Trade Centre, a trade consultancy based in Singapore. “The nightmare scenario for firms might not even involve the government. What happens if Chinese consumers start boycotting American products? Stop drinking Starbucks? Wanting iPhones?” “Between now and then, the government can easily ask for more careful customs inspections, look over documentation more slowly and enforce a myriad of rules on the books that are never used.”
That $550B figure is much larger than US exports to China, which Trump argued made China much more vulnerable to a trade war compared to the US. However:
The U.S.-China Business Council, which represents American companies that do business in China, said the market is actually much larger than just $130 billion in goods exports that the Trump administration appears to be most focused on. U.S. companies also exported about $60 billion in services to China last year and $40 billion worth of goods to Hong Kong, much of which finds its way into China. On top of that, American companies with operations in China sell hundreds of billions of dollars worth of goods and services to their Chinese customers. When all that is combined, China is about a $550 billion market for American firms, said Erin Ennis, senior vice president at the U.S.-China Business Council.
We aren't there yet, but we aren't all that far away either. The assumption underlying the US negotiating position (insofar as there is a unified one) seems to be that trade partners will cave first and can be browbeaten into concessions.
We very much doubt whether that is the case. We already see a sort of rallying of the troops in Canada and Mexico in response to US pressures. China could very easily manufacture something similar.
This stuff could become especially ugly for some US corporations that are disproportionally exposed to the Chinese market, like for instance Qualcomm ( QCOM ), Apple ( AAPL ), Walmart ( WMT ), Ford ( F ) and General Motors ( GM ).
Selling US bonds It is often argued that China could cease to buy US Treasuries (which are in most part a recycling of its trade surplus with the US), or even unload its stock of US debt altogether as a way to retaliate US tariffs and this would hurt the US economy seriously through raising bond yields.
The US economy appears to be especially vulnerable, now that there are at least two other big sellers of US debt, the Fed (unwinding QE holdings) and the Treasury itself, financing the widening budget deficit.
Would the resulting wave of selling overwhelm the bond markets, send rates up sky-high and rock the US economy, perhaps even produce a recession? Well, not necessarily.
China does hold a large stock of US Treasuries, roughly about $1.3T (including holdings via a 'Belgian' account). Brad Setser has used the QE literature to assess the impact on long-term rates should the Chinese liquidate their holdings, from Setser:
Using the "QE" literature to estimate the impact of Chinese "QT," those sales in the first instance would be estimated to raise long-term interest rates by say 30 basis points.
That really isn't terribly high, and it assumes no countering Fed reaction, which isn't very realistic. The Fed could:
Slow its pace of future interest rate rises (and hence lower long-bond yields, as these are a function of expected future Federal Funds rates). It could even lower rates, as it happens (if the economy slows down a lot). Reduce the pace of its own unwinding of its bond purchases, stop it altogether or even start purchasing Treasuries again. So basically the effects are not terrible and the Fed could counter much of these. This isn't a serious threat.
What's more, selling its Treasury stock is liable to contract Chinese domestic monetary conditions, which could very well have negative effects for China itself.
These effects could be compounded by a rise in the Chinese currency, the renminbi, which brings us to the most effective way (in our view) that China could counteract.
Devaluing the currency China has long been argued as being a currency manipulator, heavily buying dollars in order to keep its own currency low and its exports competitive. Indeed. this way, it has amassed a cool $4T in foreign currency reserves.
But all this started to change three years ago when China was hit by capital flight and in fact the PBoC, the Peoples Bank of China (its central bank) started to reverse interventions in the forex markets, now heavily buying back its own currency in order to support its external value.
As a result, panic broke out at two junctures in the world's financial markets when the Chinese capital flight seemed to accelerate and investors pondered how long the PBoC could maintain its interventions and what the economic consequences of a large Chinese devaluation would be.
The biggest of these selloffs occurred at the start of 2016, as you can see in the chart above (there was an earlier scare in the late summer of the previous year).
In the process, the PBoC quickly lost $1T of its foreign currency reserves in short order:
You also see that the forex reserves have started to stabilize and even recover mildly last year (although part of that is due to the dollar falling versus other main currencies like the euro, as the Chinese authorities calculate their forex reserves on a dollar basis) as the great China scare subsided. Capital controls and tightening monetary policy managed to stem the rot.
What one also might realize is the fact that China has already lost much of its once huge trade surplus:
By 2011, this was already down to a rather modest 2% of GDP and last year it was even lower at just 1.5%. This is mostly an effect of the great domestic stimulus programs in the wake of the 2008/9 financial crisis, which boosted Chinese domestic spending and hence imports (helping the world economy to recover in the process).
The yuan, which was strengthening all of last year and reached a high of 6.25 per US dollar back in April, is already falling again.
But a falling currency is a recent phenomenon. Until recently, a rising currency combined with higher wage growth (as demographics make labor more scarce) compared to most of its trading partners was eroding Chinese competitiveness, here is The Economist back in 2015:
Since 2001, hourly manufacturing wages in China have risen by an average of 12% a year. The yuan has risen to an all-time high against a trade-weighted basket of currencies.
Automation, moving factories inwards and squeezing margins can keep the Chinese manufacturing show running for quite some time, but the downward trend has already set in:
Today, the Chinese could, in response to US pressures, let its currency slip in order to recoup any lost trade due to US tariffs. This isn't very difficult, as it happens:
China could relax its monetary policy (in fact, it's doing just that , as of Monday morning June 25). It could relax some of the stringent capital controls it introduced in order to curb the 2014-6 capital outflows. It could start buying dollars in the forex markets again. One could call this even a sort of a China first policy, as it seems to offer considerable benefits for China itself (unless they lose control over the process).
We think the only thing holding the authorities back is that the trade conflict isn't yet on boiling point and China is also afraid it will reactivate the uncontrolled capital flight of a couple of years ago.
So we think this is something the Chinese keep in their playing deck of cards, and will only release it in a very controlled manner and in response to a substantial escalation of the trade tensions.
The effects could be quite devastating. We have seen how financial markets all over the world reacted to an earlier episode (which we referenced above), as this has the potential to unleash a deflationary wave onto the world economy that could very well tip it over into recession.
Conclusion Should the US further escalate the trade tensions with China, the latter is not likely to cave. In fact, despite the asymmetric nature of the trade relations, China has more weapons at its disposal than just slapping tariffs on American imports.
It could make life very difficult for US corporations operating in China, which is potentially bad news for the stocks of the companies involved.
In extremis, China could manufacture a controlled devaluation to make up for US tariffs on its exports. For investors, this is the most dangerous scenario, as this could unleash a deflationary wave on the world economy which could have serious consequences for world growth and financial markets.
Disclosure: I/we have no positions in any stocks mentioned, and no plans to initiate any positions within the next 72 hours.
